questions.q: How does "done" typically differ between a product engineer and a research engineer?
options: There is no difference; both mean the same thing
Product "done" means working for every user indefinitely; research "done" often means producing a trustworthy number once
Research "done" always requires more testing than product "done"
Product engineers never ship anything considered "done"
questions.explain: Product code must hold up for every future user under load. Research code frequently only needs to produce one trustworthy result for the experiment at hand.

questions.q: Why does research engineering spend less effort on edge-case handling than product engineering?
options: Because research engineers are less skilled
Because edge cases never occur in machine learning
Because the cost structure is different — time spent handling edge cases you'll never hit is time not spent running another experiment
Because research code is never run more than once
questions.explain: This is a deliberate trade-off, not sloppiness: in research, unused defensive code is a real opportunity cost against running more experiments.

questions.q: What makes a research bug typically harder to notice than a product bug, as described in this lesson?
options: Research bugs are always larger in scope
Research bugs usually crash the program immediately
A research bug often lets the code run to completion and produce a plausible but wrong number, rather than throwing a visible error
Research bugs only occur in compiled languages
questions.explain: Product bugs tend to be loud (errors, alarms). Research bugs are often silent — the script finishes and the number looks fine but is statistically wrong.

questions.q: Which part of a research codebase is the exception that still gets production-grade rigor, according to this lesson?
options: One-off scripts used to generate a single plot
Shared infrastructure that many experiments depend on, such as the training framework or data loader
Jupyter notebooks used for internal discussion
Nothing in a research codebase ever gets production-grade rigor
questions.explain: Shared infrastructure that many researchers build on gets production-grade testing and review, because corrupting it would invalidate every experiment that depends on it.

questions.q: Which product-engineering instinct does this lesson say can actively mislead a new research engineer?
options: Version control discipline
Debugging methodology like bisecting and isolating variables
"Abstract early for reuse," since research code's shape changes weekly as hypotheses change
Reading an unfamiliar codebase comfortably
questions.explain: Early abstraction built for last week's experiment often has to be torn out as hypotheses shift, making "abstract early" a liability rather than a virtue in research code.
